blocks.prompt: 3. Prove that \(\sum_{k=0}^{n} r^k = \frac{r^{n+1} - 1}{r - 1}\), whenever \(n\) is a positive integer. [printed with the lower limit \(k = 1\), which makes the statement false; \(r \ne 1\) is also needed]
blocks.explanation:
The symbol \(\sum_{k=0}^{n} r^k\) means \(r^0 + r^1 + r^2 + \cdots + r^n = 1 + r + \cdots + r^n\): a G.P. sum with \(n + 1\) terms.
We prove the formula for every positive integer \(n\) by induction (with \(r \ne 1\)).
Plan: write the sum in full, check \(n = 1\), then add the next term \(r^{m+1}\) and make one fraction.
steps:
Given: \(S(n): 1 + r + r^2 + \cdots + r^n = \frac{r^{n+1} - 1}{r - 1}\), \(r \ne 1\).
To prove: \(S(n)\) is true for every positive integer \(n\).
Method: Mathematical induction. The letter \(k\) is already used inside the sum, so we call the induction value \(m\). The next term after \(r^m\) is \(r^{m+1}\).

Base case: put \(n = 1\)
\[\text{L.H.S.} = r^0 + r^1 = 1 + r\]
\[\text{R.H.S.} = \dfrac{r^2 - 1}{r - 1}\]
\[= \dfrac{(r - 1)(r + 1)}{r - 1} = r + 1\]
So \(S(1)\) is true.
Why: Difference of squares, and \(r - 1 \ne 0\) may be cancelled.

Induction hypothesis: assume \(S(m)\)
\[1 + r + \cdots + r^m = \dfrac{r^{m+1} - 1}{r - 1} \quad (A)\]
Why: We suppose the formula holds for some positive integer \(m\).

Write the target \(S(m + 1)\)
\[1 + r + \cdots + r^m + r^{m+1}\]
\[= \dfrac{r^{m+2} - 1}{r - 1}\]
Why: Put \(n = m + 1\): one more term, and the power on the right becomes \(m + 2\).

Inductive step: use (A)
\[\text{L.H.S.} = \dfrac{r^{m+1} - 1}{r - 1} + r^{m+1}\]
\[= \dfrac{r^{m+1} - 1 + r^{m+1}(r - 1)}{r - 1}\]
\[= \dfrac{r^{m+1} - 1 + r^{m+2} - r^{m+1}}{r - 1}\]
\[= \dfrac{r^{m+2} - 1}{r - 1} = \text{R.H.S.}\]
Why: All terms up to \(r^m\) are replaced by (A). \(r^{m+1}\) is written over \(r - 1\); \(r^{m+1} \cdot r = r^{m+2}\); then \(r^{m+1}\) and \(-r^{m+1}\) cancel.

Conclusion
\(S(1)\) is true and \(S(m) \Rightarrow S(m + 1)\). By the principle of mathematical induction, \(\sum_{k=0}^{n} r^k = \frac{r^{n+1} - 1}{r - 1}\) for every positive integer \(n\) \((r \ne 1)\).
Why: Both conditions of the principle hold.

Check: \(r = 3,\ n = 2\)
\[1 + 3 + 9 = 13\]
\[\dfrac{3^3 - 1}{3 - 1} = \dfrac{26}{2} = 13 \;\checkmark\]
Why: Both sides agree.
blocks.final_answer: Hence proved: \(\sum_{k=0}^{n} r^k = 1 + r + \cdots + r^n = \frac{r^{n+1} - 1}{r - 1}\) for every positive integer \(n\) \((r \ne 1)\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints the lower limit of the sum as \(k = 1\): \(\sum_{k=1}^{n} r^k = \frac{r^{n+1} - 1}{r - 1}\). This statement is false: for \(n = 1\) the left side is \(r\) but the right side is \(\frac{r^2 - 1}{r - 1} = r + 1\). The formula is true when the sum starts at \(k = 0\), as proved above. (With \(k = 1\) the correct sum is \(\frac{r^{n+1} - r}{r - 1}\).) The condition \(r \ne 1\) is also needed, since \(r - 1\) is the denominator.
